etymology: From missionary, Latin mittere, to send; and journey, Old French journee, a day's travel. The term names the first recorded apostolic circuit of Acts 13—14.
biblical_def: The First Missionary Journey is the gospel circuit of Acts 13—14, in which the Holy Ghost set apart Saul and Barnabas from the church at Antioch, saying, "Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them" (Acts 13:2). Sent forth by the Spirit and commissioned by the laying on of the church's hands, they sailed to Cyprus, where Paul withstood the sorcerer Elymas and the deputy Sergius Paulus believed. Thence to Pisidian Antioch, where Paul preached Christ crucified and risen, and the Gentiles "were glad, and glorified the word of the Lord: and as many as were ordained to eternal life believed" (Acts 13:48). The Jews stirred up persecution at Iconium; at Lystra Paul healed a cripple, was hailed a god, then stoned and left for dead, yet rose and went on to Derbe. Returning, they confirmed the disciples and "ordained them elders in every church" (Acts 14:23). This journey displays the sovereign God thrusting forth His sent men, the gospel going to the Gentiles by definite election, and the planting of churches under a plurality of elders. This dictionary confesses that missions begin not in human enterprise but in the Spirit's commission through a sending church.
webster_summary: The first apostolic circuit, Acts 13—14, in which Paul and Barnabas, sent by the Holy Ghost from Antioch, carried the gospel through Cyprus and the cities of Asia Minor, planting churches and ordaining elders.
webster_full: FIRST MISSIONARY JOURNEY, noun. The first recorded circuit of apostolic preaching, Acts 13 and 14, undertaken by Paul and Barnabas.
Begun at Syrian Antioch when the Holy Ghost said, "Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them."
It compassed Cyprus, Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe, the gospel coming to the Gentiles.
It requires that messengers be sent by the Spirit through the church, and it forbids self-appointed mission apart from that commission.
Its end was churches confirmed and elders ordained, under the sanction of him who calls and sends.
scriptures: Acts 13:2
As they ministered to the Lord, and fasted, the Holy Ghost said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them.
Acts 13:48
And when the Gentiles heard this, they were glad, and glorified the word of the Lord: and as many as were ordained to eternal life believed.
Acts 14:22
Confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God.
Acts 14:23
And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the recurring danger is to sever missions from the local church and from sovereign election.
corruption_paragraphs: The chief abuse of this history is to read it as a charter for autonomous adventurism—men running before they are sent, accountable to no church, planting nothing that endures. But Luke is careful: the Spirit spoke within a worshipping congregation, the church fasted and laid on hands, and the apostles returned to report. The journey ends not with converts left to themselves but with elders ordained in every church. Missions is the church's work, extended through her sent men, not a freelance enterprise.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The positive principle to recover is that the success of the journey rested on God's decree: "as many as were ordained to eternal life believed." The same sovereign grace that hardened the gainsaying Jews opened the hearts of the Gentiles. Modern method-driven missiology, which trusts technique and numbers, must be answered by the Acts pattern—faithful preaching of Christ crucified, suffering borne with joy, and the planting of ordered churches, all under the hand of the God who calls.
roots_summary: The phrase joins Latin mittere (to send) with the journeys narrated in Acts 13—14.
roots_lines: Missionary derives from Latin mittere, missus, to send, mirroring the Greek apostello.
Journey comes through Old French journee, a day's travel or stage.
The Greek of Acts 13:2 reads aphorisate, "separate ye," the same root as set apart unto holiness.
Acts 13:3 uses apelusan, they sent away, after fasting, prayer, and the laying on of hands.
The pattern roots all true sending in the prior call and decree of the triune God.
usage: On the First Missionary Journey, Paul preached in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch before turning to the Gentiles.
The stoning of Paul at Lystra belongs to the First Missionary Journey, yet he rose and pressed on to Derbe.
The First Missionary Journey closed with elders ordained in every church and a report given to the sending congregation at Antioch.

etymology: From second, Latin secundus, following; with missionary, Latin mittere, to send. Names the apostolic circuit of Acts 15:36—18:22.
biblical_def: The Second Missionary Journey, Acts 15:36—18:22, began when Paul proposed to Barnabas that they revisit the brethren. The sharp contention over John Mark parted them, Barnabas taking Mark and Paul choosing Silas; thus two companies went forth. Paul took Timothy at Lystra, and the churches "were established in the faith, and increased in number daily" (Acts 16:5). Forbidden by the Spirit to preach in Asia and Bithynia, Paul received in the night the vision of a man of Macedonia, "Come over into Macedonia, and help us" (Acts 16:9), and the gospel crossed into Europe. At Philippi Lydia and the jailor were converted; at Thessalonica and Berea the word ran, the Bereans "searched the scriptures daily" (Acts 17:11); at Athens Paul reasoned on Mars' hill; and at Corinth he abode long, for the Lord said, "I have much people in this city" (Acts 18:10). This journey shows the providence of God shutting doors and opening them, directing His messengers by His Spirit, and gathering His elect among the nations. This dictionary confesses that the spread of the gospel into Europe was no accident of history but the ordered work of the sovereign Lord.
webster_summary: The second apostolic circuit, Acts 15:36—18:22, in which Paul, Silas, and Timothy, directed by the Macedonian vision, carried the gospel into Europe, planting churches at Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea, and Corinth.
webster_full: SECOND MISSIONARY JOURNEY, noun. The apostolic circuit of Acts 15:36 through 18:22, led by Paul with Silas and Timothy.
Occasioned by Paul's purpose to revisit the brethren, and marked by the contention over John Mark that parted Paul and Barnabas.
Directed by the night vision, "Come over into Macedonia, and help us," whereby the gospel entered Europe.
It requires that messengers follow the Spirit's leading, and it forbids presuming upon doors the Lord has shut.
Its fruit was churches at Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea, and Corinth, under the promise, "I have much people in this city."
scriptures: Acts 16:5
And so were the churches established in the faith, and increased in number daily.
Acts 16:9
And a vision appeared to Paul in the night; There stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us.
Acts 17:11
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Acts 18:10
For I am with thee, and no man shall set on thee to hurt thee: for I have much people in this city.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the standing lesson is God's sovereign direction of where and to whom the gospel goes.
corruption_paragraphs: There is no genuine modern redefinition of this history, but there is a persistent misuse: treating the Macedonian call as a template for subjective impressions divorced from Scripture, so that any private hunch is christened a divine leading. Luke shows the opposite—a Spirit-given vision joined to apostolic wisdom, sober reasoning, and confirmation in the churches. The Bereans are commended precisely because they tested even Paul's preaching against the written Word.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sovereignty of God over the geography of grace: He forbade Asia and Bithynia and called Macedonia, and He promised at Corinth, "I have much people in this city," before a single Corinthian had believed. The elect are His before they are gathered. This rebukes both the despair that says a city is too hard and the pragmatism that trusts method over the decree, and it summons the church to faithful labor where the Lord opens the door.
roots_summary: The title marks the second of Paul's recorded circuits, Acts 15:36—18:22, opened by the Macedonian vision.
roots_lines: Second is from Latin secundus, that which follows the first.
The Greek diaporeuomenoi, passing through, describes the journey across cities and provinces.
Acts 16:9 uses horama, a vision, the means by which God directed the route.
Acts 16:10 reads sumbibazontes, concluding, gathering that the Lord had called them.
The circuit roots the European church in the same gospel first preached in Asia.
usage: On the Second Missionary Journey, Paul received the Macedonian call and turned westward toward Philippi.
Timothy joined Paul at Lystra during the Second Missionary Journey and became a faithful son in the faith.
The long Corinthian ministry that closed the Second Missionary Journey rested on the Lord's word, "I have much people in this city."

etymology: Greek Makedonia, the kingdom of Philip and Alexander; later the Roman province north of Achaia in the Balkan peninsula.
biblical_def: Macedonia is the Roman province lying north of Achaia in the Greek peninsula, the first soil of Europe to receive the gospel. It was to Macedonia that Paul was summoned by the night vision, "Come over into Macedonia, and help us" (Acts 16:9), and in obedience he crossed from Troas to plant churches at Philippi, Thessalonica, and Berea. There Lydia's heart was opened, the Philippian jailor cried, "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?", and the noble Bereans "searched the scriptures daily." The Macedonian churches, though tried by deep affliction, became a wonder of liberality, for Paul testifies, "how that in a great trial of affliction the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality" (2 Cor 8:2). They gave "beyond their power" and first "gave their own selves to the Lord" (2 Cor 8:5). Thus Macedonia stands in Scripture both as the gateway of the gospel into Europe and as a pattern of grace-wrought generosity. This dictionary confesses that the same sovereign Lord who directed Paul's steps to Macedonia wrought in her poor saints a liberality that shames the rich.
webster_summary: A Roman province north of Achaia in the Greek peninsula; the first region of Europe evangelized by Paul, home to the churches of Philippi, Thessalonica, and Berea, renowned for their grace-wrought liberality.
webster_full: MACEDONIA, noun. A Roman province in the north of the Greek peninsula, above Achaia.
The first part of Europe to hear the gospel, entered by Paul after the vision, "Come over into Macedonia, and help us."
Its chief gospel cities were Philippi, Thessalonica, and Berea.
Its churches, in deep poverty, abounded in liberality: "to their power, and beyond their power they were willing of themselves."
A standing example of giving that flows first from giving one's own self to the Lord.
scriptures: Acts 16:9
And a vision appeared to Paul in the night; There stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us.
2 Cor 8:1
Moreover, brethren, we do you to wit of the grace of God bestowed on the churches of Macedonia.
2 Cor 8:2
How that in a great trial of affliction the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality.
2 Cor 8:5
And this they did, not as we hoped, but first gave their own selves to the Lord, and unto us by the will of God.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the lesson to recover is that true Christian liberality springs from grace, not surplus.
corruption_paragraphs: Macedonia is a place-name with no modern ideological redefinition, yet the modern church often inverts its lesson. The prevailing assumption is that giving follows prosperity—that men give when they have plenty. The Macedonians give the lie to this: in "deep poverty" and "great trial of affliction" their joy overflowed in liberality "beyond their power." Generosity is fruit of grace, not of abundance.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the order Paul names: they "first gave their own selves to the Lord, and unto us by the will of God." Christian liberality is not a fundraising technique but the overflow of hearts already surrendered to Christ. Where the self is given, the purse follows; where it is withheld, no campaign can manufacture the grace. Macedonia summons the affluent church to repentance and to the joy of giving that springs from grace.
roots_summary: From Greek Makedonia, the ancient kingdom and later Roman province north of Achaia.
roots_lines: Greek Makedonia named the kingdom of Philip II and Alexander the Great.
Under Rome it became a senatorial province with capital at Thessalonica.
The man of the vision is called aner Makedon, a Macedonian, in Acts 16:9.
Paul's letters to Philippi and Thessalonica address Macedonian churches directly.
The province roots the European church's beginnings in apostolic, Spirit-led missions.
usage: Paul preached in Macedonia before passing southward into Achaia and the city of Corinth.
The churches of Macedonia, though poor, gave so liberally that Paul held them up as an example to Corinth.
Lydia of Thyatira was the first convert in Macedonia, her heart opened by the Lord at Philippi.

etymology: From Macedonia, the Roman province, and call, Old English ceallian, to summon. Names the night vision of Acts 16:9—10.
biblical_def: The Macedonian Call is the night vision granted to Paul at Troas: "There stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us" (Acts 16:9). Immediately Paul and his company "endeavoured to go into Macedonia, assuredly gathering that the Lord had called us for to preach the gospel unto them" (Acts 16:10). The call came not in a vacuum but after the Spirit had "forbidden them to preach the word in Asia" and "suffered them not" to enter Bithynia (Acts 16:6—7). Thus God shut two doors and opened a third, and the gospel crossed into Europe. The Macedonian Call displays the sovereign providence of God ordering the course of missions—hindering here, beckoning there—so that the elect among the nations are reached in His appointed way and time. It is not a warrant for mysticism, for the vision was confirmed by sober apostolic judgment and joined to the preached Word. This dictionary confesses that the spread of the gospel is governed by the providence of God, who opens and shuts doors that no man can open or shut against His will.
webster_summary: The night vision of Acts 16:9—10, in which a man of Macedonia bid Paul, "Come over into Macedonia, and help us," whereby God directed the gospel into Europe after shutting the doors to Asia and Bithynia.
webster_full: MACEDONIAN CALL, noun. The night vision of Acts 16, summoning Paul into Europe.
The vision showed a man of Macedonia praying, "Come over into Macedonia, and help us."
It followed the Spirit's forbidding of Asia and Bithynia, marking God's sovereign direction of the route.
It requires that the church follow the doors God opens, and it forbids forcing the doors He shuts.
It seals the truth that providence governs the geography and timing of the gospel's advance.
scriptures: Acts 16:6
Now when they had gone throughout Phrygia and the region of Galatia, and were forbidden of the Holy Ghost to preach the word in Asia.
Acts 16:7
After they were come to Mysia, they assayed to go into Bithynia: but the Spirit suffered them not.
Acts 16:9
And a vision appeared to Paul in the night; There stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us.
Acts 16:10
And after he had seen the vision, immediately we endeavoured to go into Macedonia, assuredly gathering that the Lord had called us for to preach the gospel unto them.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is to wrench the vision into a charter for subjective "leadings" untethered from Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: The Macedonian Call has no modern ideological redefinition, but it is frequently abused as a proof-text for mysticism—the notion that the Christian should expect visions and inner promptings to guide every decision. Such use ignores the cessation of the extraordinary revelatory gifts and the fact that Paul was an apostle receiving canonical revelation. The ordinary believer is led by the sufficient Word, sober wisdom, and the providence of circumstance, not by dreams treated as oracles.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the doctrine of providence: God forbade Asia, suffered them not into Bithynia, and called them to Macedonia, governing every step. The same hand that hinders one labor opens another. This rebukes both the presumption that demands open doors and the despair that quits at the shut ones, and it teaches the church to trust the Lord who works all things after the counsel of His own will, including the advance of the gospel among the nations.
roots_summary: The phrase joins Macedonia with the apostolic call of the Acts 16 vision.
roots_lines: Call descends from Old English ceallian and Old Norse kalla, to summon or cry out.
The Greek horama, vision, names the night appearance to Paul.
Acts 16:10 uses proskeklētai, has called, the Lord summoning to the work.
The forbidding verbs kōlythentes and ouk eiasen mark the doors God shut.
The call roots the European mission in divine providence, not human strategy.
usage: The Macedonian Call turned Paul from Asia and sent the gospel across the sea into Europe.
Many missionary societies have spoken of a Macedonian Call to describe a field providentially opened.
The Macedonian Call teaches that God shuts some doors only to open a greater one.

etymology: From Latin colligere, to gather together; in Paul, the logia or gathering "for the saints" (1 Cor 16:1), a relief offering for the poor believers at Jerusalem.
biblical_def: The Collection was Paul's great gathering of relief among the Gentile churches for the poor saints at Jerusalem. He charged the Corinthians, "Upon the first day of the week let every one of you lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him" (1 Cor 16:2), and he set the churches of Macedonia and Achaia to the same grace. He named its purpose plainly: "it hath pleased them of Macedonia and Achaia to make a certain contribution for the poor saints which are at Jerusalem" (Rom 15:26). He grounded it in a debt of fellowship: the Gentiles, made partakers of the Jews' spiritual things, were bound "to minister unto them in carnal things" (Rom 15:27). In 2 Corinthians 8—9 Paul unfolds the whole grace of giving—the Macedonians' liberality in poverty, the example of Christ who "though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor," and the promise that "God loveth a cheerful giver." Thus the Collection sealed the unity of Jew and Gentile in one body, the wall broken down, fellowship proved by liberality. This dictionary confesses that Christian giving is a grace wrought by God, an act of worship, and a bond of love between the members of Christ's church.
webster_summary: Paul's relief offering gathered among the Gentile churches for the poor saints at Jerusalem; the great New Testament instance of the grace of giving and a seal of Jew-Gentile fellowship.
webster_full: THE COLLECTION, noun. Paul's gathering of funds among the Gentile churches for the poor saints at Jerusalem.
Ordered on the first day of the week, "as God hath prospered him."
Named in Romans 15:26 as "a certain contribution for the poor saints which are at Jerusalem."
It requires cheerful, proportionate, grace-wrought giving, and it forbids constraint and grudging.
It sealed the fellowship of Jew and Gentile in one body and proved love by liberality.
scriptures: Now concerning the collection for the saints, as I have given order to the churches of Galatia, even so do ye.
Upon the first day of the week let every one of you lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him, that there be no gatherings when I come.
For it hath pleased them of Macedonia and Achaia to make a certain contribution for the poor saints which are at Jerusalem.
2 Cor 9:7
Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the lesson is the recovery of giving as grace and worship rather than as obligation or sentiment.
corruption_paragraphs: The Collection is not the subject of modern ideological dispute, yet its doctrine is widely flattened. Some reduce giving to mere fundraising and pressure; others, reacting, treat it as wholly optional and unstructured. Paul holds both error in check: the giving is ordered ("upon the first day of the week"), proportionate ("as God hath prospered him"), and free ("not grudgingly, or of necessity"). It is neither a tax wrung by guilt nor a whim left to mood, but a grace.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the theological weight Paul places on the Collection: it is grounded in the example of Christ, who became poor to make many rich, and it is the proof of fellowship between Jew and Gentile in one body. Giving to the saints is service rendered to Christ Himself and a visible bond of the church's unity. To recover this is to see the offering not as the price of admission to worship but as an act of worship flowing from grace received.
roots_summary: From Latin colligere, to gather; in Paul the logia of relief for the Jerusalem poor.
roots_lines: Latin colligere, collectus, to gather together, yields English collection.
Paul's word in 1 Cor 16:1 is logia, a collection or gathering of money.
In 2 Cor 8—9 he calls it charis, grace, and diakonia, ministry.
He names it also koinōnia, the fellowship of the saints in giving.
The terms root Christian liberality in grace received and fellowship expressed.
usage: Paul organized the Collection across Galatia, Macedonia, and Achaia for the relief of Jerusalem's poor saints.
The Collection proved that Gentile believers owed a debt of love to the church that first received the promises.
In teaching the Collection, Paul set forth the grace of giving and the gladness of the cheerful giver.

etymology: Gaius, a common Roman praenomen; of Derbe distinguishes this companion of Paul from the Gaius of Corinth and the Gaius of 3 John.
biblical_def: Gaius of Derbe is named among the brethren who accompanied Paul as he set out from Greece toward Jerusalem at the close of the third journey: "And there accompanied him into Asia Sopater of Berea; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timotheus" (Acts 20:4). The careful geographic tag, "of Derbe," marks him out from the Gaius of Macedonia seized in the Ephesian riot (Acts 19:29), from Gaius of Corinth whom Paul baptized and called "mine host" (Rom 16:23), and from the Gaius to whom John wrote, "the wellbeloved Gaius, whom I love in the truth" (3 John 1). Of his words and deeds Scripture is silent; he appears only as a faithful fellow-traveler, one of the delegates likely bearing the Collection to Jerusalem. Yet his quiet inclusion testifies to the host of unnamed and lightly-named laborers whom God raised up to carry the gospel and serve the apostle. This dictionary confesses that the Lord honors faithful, obscure service, recording even the names of those whose works are hidden, for He is not unrighteous to forget the labor of love shown toward His name.
webster_summary: A companion of Paul from Derbe in Lycaonia, named in Acts 20:4 among the brethren traveling toward Jerusalem; to be distinguished from the Gaius of Corinth and the Gaius of 3 John.
webster_full: GAIUS OF DERBE, noun. A fellow-traveler of Paul, of the city of Derbe in Lycaonia.
Named in Acts 20:4 among those who accompanied Paul into Asia toward Jerusalem.
Distinguished by his city from Gaius of Corinth and the Gaius addressed in the Third Epistle of John.
He appears as a faithful companion, likely a delegate bearing the relief Collection.
A witness that God records and rewards even hidden and unheralded service.
scriptures: Acts 20:4
And there accompanied him into Asia Sopater of Berea; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timotheus; and of Asia, Tychicus and Trophimus.
Acts 19:29
And the whole city was filled with confusion: and having caught Gaius and Aristarchus, men of Macedonia, Paul's companions in travel, they rushed with one accord into the theatre.
Gaius mine host, and of the whole church, saluteth you. Erastus the chamberlain of the city saluteth you, and Quartus a brother.
3 John 1:1
The elder unto the wellbeloved Gaius, whom I love in the truth.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the point is recovering the honor of obscure faithfulness and careful attention to Scripture's distinctions.
corruption_paragraphs: There is no modern controversy over Gaius of Derbe, but careless readers conflate the several men named Gaius in the New Testament. Sound interpretation observes the Spirit's own distinctions: the city tag "of Derbe" is given precisely to separate this man from the Macedonian Gaius of the riot, the Corinthian Gaius who hosted Paul, and the beloved Gaius of John's letter. Such care guards against the muddling of the text and honors its precision.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of hidden service. Gaius of Derbe does nothing recorded, says nothing recorded, yet the Holy Ghost preserves his name forever as a faithful companion of the apostle. The modern craving for platform and visibility is rebuked by such a man, whose reward is not in being seen but in serving Christ. God is not unrighteous to forget any labor of love, however small or unseen, done toward His name.
roots_summary: Gaius is a Roman praenomen; Derbe a city of Lycaonia evangelized on the first journey.
roots_lines: Gaius was among the most common Roman first names, borne by several New Testament men.
Derbe lay in Lycaonia, reached by Paul and Barnabas on the first missionary journey.
Acts 20:4 lists him among the delegates accompanying Paul, the Greek suneipeto, went with.
The qualifier Derbaios, of Derbe, fixes his origin and distinguishes him from others.
The name roots him among the company of faithful, lightly-recorded gospel laborers.
usage: Gaius of Derbe traveled with Paul toward Jerusalem at the end of the third missionary journey.
Readers should not confuse Gaius of Derbe with the Gaius whom Paul baptized at Corinth.
Like Sopater and Secundus, Gaius of Derbe is a name we know with deeds we do not, a quiet servant of Christ.

etymology: John, Hebrew Yochanan, "the Lord is gracious"; Mark, Latin Marcus, his Roman surname. The two names mark his Jewish and Roman identity.
biblical_def: John, whose surname was Mark, was the son of Mary of Jerusalem, in whose house the church gathered to pray when Peter was delivered from prison (Acts 12:12). He was kinsman to Barnabas and went with Paul and Barnabas as their minister on the first journey, but at Pamphylia "John departing from them returned to Jerusalem" (Acts 13:13). When Barnabas would take him again, the contention was so sharp that Paul and Barnabas parted, "and so Barnabas took Mark, and sailed unto Cyprus" (Acts 15:39). Yet this was not the end of the man. Grace restored him: Paul later names Mark among his fellow-labourers, and at the last writes, "Take Mark, and bring him with thee: for he is profitable to me for the ministry" (2 Tim 4:11). Peter calls him "Marcus my son" (1 Pet 5:13), and the church has ever received him as the writer of the second Gospel. Thus John Mark is a standing testimony of restoration after failure. This dictionary confesses that the Lord does not cast off His servants for a single faltering, but in His grace recovers and reuses those who once turned back, making the unprofitable profitable for the ministry.
webster_summary: The son of Mary of Jerusalem and kinsman of Barnabas, whose desertion at Pamphylia occasioned the Paul-Barnabas contention; later restored as profitable for the ministry, and the writer of the Gospel of Mark.
webster_full: JOHN MARK, noun. The son of Mary of Jerusalem, kinsman of Barnabas, and writer of the second Gospel.
First seen in Acts 12:12, where the church prayed in his mother's house for Peter's release.
He departed from Paul and Barnabas at Pamphylia, occasioning their sharp contention.
Restored by grace, he became one of whom Paul wrote, "he is profitable to me for the ministry."
Peter called him "Marcus my son," and through him the Gospel of Mark was given to the church.
scriptures: Acts 12:12
And when he had considered the thing, he came to the house of Mary the mother of John, whose surname was Mark; where many were gathered together praying.
Acts 13:13
Now when Paul and his company loosed from Paphos, they came to Perga in Pamphylia: and John departing from them returned to Jerusalem.
Acts 15:39
And the contention was so sharp between them, that they departed asunder one from the other: and so Barnabas took Mark, and sailed unto Cyprus.
Only Luke is with me. Take Mark, and bring him with thee: for he is profitable to me for the ministry.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the lesson is the recovery of biblical restoration after failure, neither excusing the fault nor despairing of the man.
corruption_paragraphs: John Mark is not the subject of modern ideological dispute, but his story is often mishandled in two directions. Some excuse his desertion as nothing, dissolving the seriousness that made Paul refuse to take him again; others harden it into a permanent verdict, as if a man who once turned back could never be useful. Scripture allows neither. The departure was a real fault, grievous enough to part two great men; yet it was not final, for grace restored him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the doctrine of restoration. The God who perseveres with His own does not discard them for a single failure; He chastens, recovers, and reuses. Mark, once the cause of contention and called by implication unprofitable, ends as "profitable to me for the ministry" and the penman of a Gospel. This rebukes both the leniency that winks at desertion and the rigor that writes men off, and it comforts every faltering servant with the certainty that the Lord finishes the work He begins.
roots_summary: John renders Hebrew Yochanan, the Lord is gracious; Mark is the Latin Marcus.
roots_lines: John is the Hebrew Yochanan, "the Lord is gracious," his Jewish name.
Mark is the Latin Marcus, his Roman surname, fitting a dweller in the Empire.
Acts 13:5 calls him their hupēretēs, minister or attendant, on the first journey.
Acts 13:13 uses apochōrēsas, having departed, of his turning back at Pamphylia.
His double name roots him in both the covenant people and the wider Gentile world he served.
usage: John Mark turned back at Pamphylia, but grace later restored him to fruitful ministry.
The contention over John Mark parted Paul and Barnabas at the start of the second journey.
Peter's affection for John Mark, "Marcus my son," shaped the Gospel that bears his name.

etymology: From send, Old English sendan, to cause to go; rendering Greek apostellō. The sending church is the local body that commissions missionaries.
biblical_def: The Sending Church is the local congregation that, under Christ's authority, commissions and supports those whom the Spirit calls to the work of the gospel. The pattern is Antioch: "the Holy Ghost said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them. And when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away" (Acts 13:2—3). The call originated with the Spirit, but the commissioning was the act of a worshipping local church—fasting, praying, the laying on of hands, the sending. When the work was done, the missionaries returned to Antioch, "from whence they had been recommended to the grace of God for the work which they fulfilled" (Acts 14:26), and "rehearsed all that God had done with them." Thus missionaries are sent men, accountable to the church that sent them, not autonomous agents. This stands against the modern parachurch model that sends apart from any local church's oversight, and against the lone freelancer who answers to none. This dictionary confesses that the Great Commission is given to the church, and that the right ordering of missions is the local congregation, governed by its elders, sending and sustaining the men whom the Lord has called.
webster_summary: The local congregation that, under Christ's authority and through its elders, commissions and supports missionaries; modeled by Antioch in Acts 13, which fasted, prayed, laid on hands, and sent forth Barnabas and Saul.
webster_full: THE SENDING CHURCH, noun. The local congregation that commissions and supports those called to the gospel work.
Modeled by Antioch, which set apart Barnabas and Saul at the Spirit's word.
It acted by fasting, prayer, the laying on of hands, and the sending away of its men.
It requires that missionaries be sent and held accountable by a local church, and it forbids autonomous, churchless sending.
Its returning men "rehearsed all that God had done," sealing their accountability to the body.
scriptures: Acts 13:1

Now there were in the church that was at Antioch certain prophets and teachers; as Barnabas, and Simeon that was called Niger, and Lucius of Cyrene, and Manaen, which had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul.
Acts 13:3
And when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away.
Acts 14:26
And thence sailed to Antioch, from whence they had been recommended to the grace of God for the work which they fulfilled.
Acts 14:27
And when they were come, and had gathered the church together, they rehearsed all that God had done with them, and how he had opened the door of faith unto the Gentiles.
corruption_summary: The modern corruption is the autonomous parachurch and freelance model that sends and supports missionaries apart from the oversight of a local church.
corruption_paragraphs: The prevailing corruption is the divorce of missions from the local church. Whole agencies send, support, and govern missionaries with no congregation standing behind them, and many a sincere worker goes out as a lone freelancer accountable to no eldership. The Antioch pattern rebukes this. The Spirit's call came within a worshipping church; the church fasted, prayed, laid on hands, and sent; and the sent men returned to report. Missions is not a private vocation pursued beside the church but a work of the church, extended through her commissioned men.

This is not to deny that believers may cooperate across congregations, for the churches of Macedonia and Achaia joined in the Collection. But cooperation must not displace oversight. The right ordering keeps each missionary anchored in a sending church, governed by elders, sustained and held to account by the body. To recover the Sending Church is to recover the Great Commission as Christ gave it—to His church—and to put an end to the rootless sending that has too often loosed men from the discipline and the prayers of the saints.
roots_summary: From Old English sendan, to cause to go, rendering the Greek apostellō, to send forth.
roots_lines: Send is from Old English sendan, to cause to go on a journey or mission.
It renders the Greek apostellō, to send forth with a commission, the root of apostle.
Acts 13:3 uses apelusan, they sent away, after prayer and laying on of hands.
Acts 14:26 uses paradedomenoi, having been committed or recommended to the grace of God.
The terms root missionary sending in the deliberate, ordered act of a local church.
usage: Antioch is the model of the Sending Church, fasting and praying before it sent Barnabas and Saul.
A missionary without a Sending Church to commission and sustain him departs from the Acts pattern.
The Sending Church holds its missionaries accountable, even as Paul and Barnabas returned to rehearse what God had done.

etymology: From Greek diakonia, service or ministration, rendered ministry; the service rendered to the saints, the household of faith.
biblical_def: Ministry to the Saints is the diakonia, the practical service, rendered by believers to their fellow believers as members of one body. Paul went up to Jerusalem "to minister unto the saints" (Rom 15:25), carrying the relief of the Gentile churches to the poor brethren there. He commends the house of Stephanas, "that they have addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints" (1 Cor 16:15), and he assures the Hebrews that "God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love, which ye have shewed toward his name, in that ye have ministered to the saints, and do minister" (Heb 6:10). Such ministry is no incidental kindness but the very fruit of saving grace, the love that proves a living faith. It is service rendered to Christ Himself, for what is done to the least of His brethren is done unto Him. Distinct from the world's philanthropy, it is directed first to the household of God, "especially unto them who are of the household of faith" (Gal 6:10). This dictionary confesses that genuine ministry to the saints flows from regenerate hearts, is wrought by the Spirit, and is so esteemed by God that He counts it done unto His own name.
webster_summary: The practical service (diakonia) rendered by believers to fellow believers as members of one body; a fruit of grace which God Himself esteems as labor of love shown toward His name.
webster_full: MINISTRY TO THE SAINTS, noun. The practical service rendered by believers to their fellow believers.
Exemplified by Paul going to Jerusalem "to minister unto the saints" with the relief Collection.
Seen also in the house of Stephanas, "addicted" to the ministry of the saints.
It requires love proved in deed toward the household of faith, and it forbids a faith barren of works.
God counts it "love, which ye have shewed toward his name," and is not unrighteous to forget it.
scriptures: But now I go unto Jerusalem to minister unto the saints.
I beseech you, brethren, (ye know the house of Stephanas, that it is the firstfruits of Achaia, and that they have addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints,).
Heb 6:10
For God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love, which ye have shewed toward his name, in that ye have ministered to the saints, and do minister.
Gal 6:10
As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is to dissolve Christian service into mere humanitarianism that loses its God-ward and church-ward direction.
corruption_paragraphs: There is no ideological redefinition of this doctrine, but it is often diluted. The modern impulse is to collapse ministry to the saints into generic humanitarianism, as though serving anyone for any reason were the same thing. Scripture orders the love: "especially unto them who are of the household of faith." While believers are to do good unto all men, their first and peculiar obligation is to the brethren, the members of Christ's body, the saints with whom they share one Lord, one faith, one baptism.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the God-ward weight of such service: it is "labour of love, which ye have shewed toward his name." What is done to the saints is reckoned as done to Christ, and God is not unrighteous to forget it. This lifts the meanest act of service—the meal carried, the burden borne, the gift sent—into an act of worship, performed unto the Lord and remembered by Him. To recover this is to see Christian charity not as detached benevolence but as the living fruit of grace within the body.
roots_summary: From Greek diakonia, service or ministration, directed to the hagioi, the saints.
roots_lines: Ministry renders the Greek diakonia, service, ministration, the work of a diakonos.
Saints renders hagioi, the holy ones, those set apart unto God in Christ.
Rom 15:25 uses the verb diakonōn, ministering, of Paul's service with the relief.
Heb 6:10 names it ergon and kopos tēs agapēs, work and labour of love.
The terms root such service in grace received and directed first to the household of faith.
usage: Paul's ministry to the saints carried the Gentile churches' relief to the poor believers at Jerusalem.
The house of Stephanas gave themselves to the ministry of the saints as the firstfruits of Achaia.
God remembers every act of ministry to the saints as love shown toward His own name.

etymology: From Latin mutuus, reciprocal; with ministry, Greek diakonia, service. Names the reciprocal service of believers, the "one another" of the New Testament.
biblical_def: Mutual Ministry is the reciprocal service that the members of Christ's body render one to another under the oversight of their elders. The New Testament is filled with the "one anothers"—love one another, bear one another's burdens, edify one another, exhort one another daily. Paul teaches that the gifts differ, "having then gifts differing according to the grace that is given to us" (Rom 12:6), and that the body is knit together so that "the whole body... by that which every joint supplieth... maketh increase of the body" (Eph 4:16). Yet this every-member service is not an egalitarian leveling of the offices. The same Christ who gives gifts to all gave also "some, pastors and teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry" (Eph 4:11—12). The members minister to one another; the ordained elders oversee, rule, and feed the flock. Mutual ministry therefore flourishes under, not against, the ordered offices of the church. This dictionary confesses that every member of the body has a service to render, and that this body-life is ordered by Christ under a plurality of elders, the two offices of elder and deacon remaining distinct and unleveled.
webster_summary: The reciprocal "one another" service of every member of Christ's body, exercised under the oversight of elders; not an egalitarian leveling of the offices but body-life ordered by the gifts Christ distributes.
webster_full: MUTUAL MINISTRY, noun. The reciprocal service of the members of Christ's body, one toward another.
Expressed in the New Testament "one anothers": love, edify, exhort, and bear one another's burdens.
Grounded in differing gifts, "according to the grace that is given to us."
It requires every member to serve, yet it forbids the leveling of the ordained offices.
It flourishes under the oversight of elders, whom Christ gave for the perfecting of the saints.
scriptures: Eph 4:11
And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers.
Eph 4:16

From whom the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part, maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love.
Rom 12:5
So we, being many, are one body in Christ, and every one members one of another.
As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God.
corruption_summary: The modern corruption flattens the "one anothers" into an egalitarian leveling that erases the ordained offices and the male-only eldership Christ appointed.
corruption_paragraphs: The chief abuse of mutual ministry is to wield the "one another" texts as a battering ram against the ordained offices. It is argued that since every member ministers, no member rules; that since all have gifts, none have authority; that the eldership is but a function any may assume. This egalitarian leveling contradicts the very passages it claims. Ephesians 4 in one breath speaks of every joint supplying and of the pastors and teachers Christ gave for the perfecting of the saints. The body's mutual service and the elders' oversight are not rivals but a single ordered design.

This leveling commonly carries a further error: the denial of male-only eldership. Where the offices are dissolved into undifferentiated gifting, the creational headship Christ ordained is swept away, and women are placed in the ruling and teaching office Scripture reserves to qualified men. The recovery is to hold both truths Christ joined: every member has a real and needed service to render, and the church is governed by a plurality of qualified male elders, with deacons serving alongside, the two offices distinct. Mutual ministry is the rich body-life of the saints under, never against, the order their Head appointed.
roots_summary: From Latin mutuus, reciprocal, and Greek diakonia, service; the "one another" life of the body.
roots_lines: Mutual is from Latin mutuus, reciprocal, given and received in turn.
Ministry renders Greek diakonia, service rendered to others.
The reciprocal force lies in the Greek allēlōn, "one another," recurring through the epistles.
Rom 12:6 grounds it in charismata, gifts of grace differing among the members.
The terms root body-life in grace distributed by Christ and ordered under His appointed offices.
usage: Mutual ministry calls every member to edify, exhort, and bear the burdens of the others.
The "one another" commands describe mutual ministry, not a leveling of the eldership.
Healthy mutual ministry flourishes under the oversight of a plurality of elders, not apart from it.
